q: What is a credit report?
r: A record of a person's borrowing and repayment history
Lenders use it to judge risk.
w: A list of the person's monthly grocery purchases
Credit reports track loans, not groceries.
A tax return filed with the government
A statement of the person's employer's profits
It tracks the person's credit, not a company's profits.

q: What does the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) do?
r: Protects the accuracy and privacy of consumer credit information
Consumers can dispute errors.
w: Sets the interest rates banks must charge
It does not set interest rates.
Bans the use of credit cards for travel
It does not restrict card use.

q: How often can a consumer get a free copy of their credit report from each major bureau?
r: At least once a year
Free reports are available at annualcreditreport.com.
w: Free annual reports are a legal right.
The right is at least yearly.
Only after being denied credit twice
The yearly right does not require denial.

q: What does the Truth in Lending Act (TILA) require lenders to disclose?
r: The cost of credit, including the APR and finance charges
Disclosures let borrowers compare offers.

q: What is the annual percentage rate (APR)?
r: The yearly cost of borrowing, including interest and certain fees
It lets borrowers compare loans.
w: The amount of the first payment
The length of the loan in years

q: What does the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) prohibit?
r: Discrimination in lending based on race, sex, age or marital status
Lenders must evaluate creditworthiness fairly.

q: What does the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) restrict?
r: Abusive, deceptive or harassing behavior by debt collectors
Collectors cannot threaten or harass.

q: A debt collector calls a borrower at 11 p.m. and threatens arrest for an unpaid credit card bill. What is the best description?
r: A likely violation of the FDCPA
Late calls and false threats are prohibited.
w: A legal and normal collection step
A requirement of the credit contract
The contract cannot allow illegal behavior.
Bankruptcy law does not permit this.

q: What is bankruptcy?
r: A legal process for people or businesses that cannot repay their debts
Federal courts handle it.
w: A tax paid by wealthy individuals
A method of avoiding all taxes

q: What is Chapter 7 bankruptcy?
r: Liquidation, where non-exempt assets are sold to pay creditors
Remaining eligible debts may be discharged.
w: A repayment plan lasting three to five years
It is not a tax program.

q: What is Chapter 11 bankruptcy mainly used for?
r: Reorganizing a business so it can keep operating
The debtor proposes a repayment plan.
w: It is not a tax program.

q: What is Chapter 13 bankruptcy?
r: A court-approved repayment plan for individuals with regular income
Payments are spread over three to five years.
w: A sale of all of a business's assets

q: What does an automatic stay do in bankruptcy?
r: Temporarily stops most collection actions against the debtor
It begins when the case is filed.
w: Cancels all of the debtor's debts instantly
Prevents the debtor from filing taxes

q: What is a discharge in bankruptcy?
r: A court order releasing the debtor from liability for certain debts
The debtor no longer owes those debts.
w: A fine paid to the court
A new loan from the court

q: Which debt is generally NOT discharged in bankruptcy?
r: Most student loans and recent taxes
Special rules limit their discharge.
w: Credit card debt is generally dischargeable.

q: What is a lien?
r: A legal claim on property as security for a debt
The property may be sold to satisfy the debt.

q: What is a mechanic's lien?
r: A claim by a contractor or supplier against property for unpaid work
It helps ensure payment for improvements.
w: A claim by a car owner against a mechanic
It is a claim by those who did the work.

q: What is garnishment?
r: A court-ordered withholding of part of a debtor's wages to pay a debt
Limits protect part of the wages.

q: What is a mortgage?
r: A loan secured by real estate
The lender may foreclose if payments stop.
w: A loan secured by a car

q: What is foreclosure?
r: The lender's legal process to take and sell property after loan default
It usually follows missed mortgage payments.
w: The sale of a home by choice with no debt

q: What does the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) mainly do?
r: Requires disclosure of closing costs in home purchases
It also restricts kickbacks.

q: What is a usury law?
r: A law limiting the maximum interest a lender may charge
States set limits on rates.
w: A law requiring banks to lend more
A law setting minimum interest rates

q: What is the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)?
r: An agency that insures bank deposits up to a set limit
The standard limit is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
w: An agency that collects income taxes

q: What is the standard FDIC insurance amount per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category?
r: Deposits up to this amount are insured.
w: This is lower than the limit.
This is higher than the limit.

q: What does the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regulate?
r: Securities markets and public company disclosures
It protects investors.

q: What is insider trading?
r: Trading securities based on material non-public information
It is illegal.
w: A broker placing a customer's order

q: A manager learns privately that her company will be acquired next week and buys its stock before the announcement. What is this?
r: Illegal insider trading
She used material non-public information.

q: What does the Sarbanes-Oxley Act require of public companies?
r: Stronger internal controls and accurate financial reporting
It was passed after major accounting scandals.
w: It does not set tax rates.

q: What is a tax?
r: A compulsory payment to government to fund public services
Laws set rates and rules.
w: A voluntary donation to a charity
A fee for a private service

q: What is a progressive tax system?
r: Higher incomes are taxed at higher rates
The federal income tax is an example.
w: All incomes are taxed at the same rate
Lower incomes are taxed at higher rates

q: What is a regressive tax?
r: A tax that takes a larger share of income from lower earners
Sales taxes are often called regressive.
w: A tax that takes more from higher earners
A tax that is the same percent of income for everyone
A tax that no one pays
It is a tax paid by many.

q: Who collects federal income taxes?
r: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
It is part of the Treasury Department.

q: What is tax withholding?
r: Employers deducting income tax from paychecks and sending it to the government
It spreads payment across the year.
w: A business keeping its tax money
Taxes must be sent to the government.

q: What is the penalty risk of filing taxes late without an extension?
r: Failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties plus interest
Costs grow with time.
w: Late filing does not lower taxes.

q: What is tax evasion?
r: Illegally hiding income or lying to reduce taxes
It can bring criminal charges.

q: What is a sales tax?
r: A tax added to the price of goods and services at purchase
Sellers collect it for the state or local government.
w: That is estate or inheritance tax.

q: What is a use tax?
r: A tax on goods bought out of state and used in the home state
It prevents avoiding sales tax by shopping elsewhere.
w: A tax on using public roads
That is a fuel or toll charge.
A tax on leased cars only
It is not limited to leases.
A tax on using a bank
It is not a bank tax.

q: What is a property tax based on?
r: The assessed value of real estate
Local governments set rates.

q: What is an estate tax?
r: A tax on the transfer of a deceased person's property
Large estates may owe it.
w: A tax on buying real estate
That is a transfer or sales-related tax.
A tax on selling a business
That is a capital gains matter.

q: What is a payroll tax?
r: A tax on wages used to fund programs like Social Security and Medicare
Employers and employees share these.

q: What are FICA taxes?
r: Social Security and Medicare taxes withheld from pay
The employer matches the employee's share.

q: An employee earns $4,000 a month. FICA is 7.65% for the employee. What is the monthly employee FICA withholding?
What is a tax deduction?
r: An amount subtracted from income before the tax is calculated
It lowers taxable income.
w: An amount subtracted from tax after it is calculated

q: Which is generally tax deductible for a business?
r: Ordinary and necessary business expenses
Rent and supplies are examples.

q: What is an LLC for tax purposes by default?
r: A pass-through entity, with profits taxed on owners' returns
It may elect another tax status.
w: A company that pays no taxes ever
It is a private business form.
An LLC is not automatically a nonprofit.

q: What is the difference between a tax audit and a tax lien?
r: An audit reviews a return; a lien is a legal claim on property for unpaid tax
One checks accuracy, the other secures payment.
w: An audit is a bank loan; a lien is a refund
Both are rewards for filing early

q: What is a tax-exempt organization?
r: A group that is not required to pay certain taxes, such as many charities
Qualified nonprofits may apply for status.
w: A business that never files forms
A group that has no members
A government office that sells stocks
It is not a seller of stocks.

q: Which section of the tax code is commonly associated with 501(c)(3) organizations?
r: Charitable, religious and educational nonprofits
Donations may be tax deductible.

q: What is an installment agreement with the IRS?
r: A plan to pay tax debt over time in monthly payments
It lets taxpayers avoid immediate collection.
w: It is a payment plan, not a refund.
A rule that cancels the debt

q: What is identity theft?
r: Using someone else's personal information to commit fraud
It can damage credit and finances.
w: Updating your address with the bank

q: What is the first step after discovering identity theft?
r: Place a fraud alert or freeze on credit and report it
Acting quickly limits damage.
w: Wait several months to see what happens
Share your password with the bank's caller
Do not share passwords with unsolicited callers.
